evals.prompt: Complete the game-of-life coding exercise in coding-exercises-main/game-of-life using executable-stories, and teach me how you solved it as you go. Tasks 1-3 and the edge-handling are the core; skip the animation task.
evals.expected_output: src/exercises/game-of-life/{game-of-life.ts, game-of-life.story.test.ts}, all stories green, reports/game-of-life.html regenerated, narration that reads as a TDD tutorial (seams, ordered slices, red then green per slice, prediction questions, wrap-up).
assertions: Each of the four README rules (under-population, survival with 2-3, overcrowding >3, birth with exactly 3) has its own scenario whose title or steps name the rule
Edge/boundary behaviour (cells on the grid edge or corner) is covered by at least one scenario with an explicit stated assumption (e.g. dead beyond edges or wrap-around)
A single-iteration step over a whole grid is tested with a concrete before/after grid taken from a known pattern (e.g. blinker) rather than a value computed by the implementation
Every it() in the story test file calls story.init(task) with the task argument
All tests in the exercise story file pass (test runner exit 0, zero failures)
An HTML report for the exercise was produced by the StoryReporter (an .html file in outputs/ containing the scenario titles)
Teaching prose is captured as story doc entries: at least 3 calls among story.section / story.code / story.mermaid / story.table / story.note in the test file
The story test file never calls story.state or story.screenshot (those derive a Storyboard filmstrip)
story.feature includes a glossary with at least one domain term from the README
Money or world-state snapshots in the story file are story.table (Who/Before/After or equivalent), not a pair of story.kv lines that restate the step
narration.md opens with a plan that names the public interface (seams) and lists ordered behaviour slices BEFORE any implementation code is shown
narration.md shows a failing (red) test run result before the corresponding passing (green) run for at least 3 separate slices
narration.md contains at least one prediction question posed to the learner before a result is revealed (e.g. Before we run it ... what do you expect)
narration.md ends with a wrap-up: a table or list of slices with status, and key takeaways
No assertion in the test file is tautological (expected values are literals or hand-worked from the README, never recomputed by calling the implementation or the same formula)
